children: OpenAI said it was making its advanced cybersecurity models available to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, helping the military alliance protect its networks from increasingly sophisticated threats.

The ChatGPT maker said NATO's Communications and Information Agency--the alliance's technology and cyber hub with a team of over 3,000 civilian and military experts--was leveraging its artificial-intelligence models to probe suspicious activity, detect vulnerabilities, and deploy fixes.

The AI lab announced the partnership on the first day of the NATO Edge 26 conference in Turkey, saying NATO had already used up to 300 billion tokens per month as part of its cybersecurity work, in reference to the currency that AI models use to process information and create responses. The company didn't specify when NATO started using its cybersecurity models.

As geopolitical tensions remain elevated, the alliance is grappling with increasingly sophisticated threats, particularly in cyberspace: a cyberattack recently targeted European supermarket refrigerators and freezers, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage from spoiled food and equipment failures.

Meanwhile, airports and airlines across the continent have been receiving a wave of hoax bomb threats via email in recent weeks, forcing authorities to divert flights and order emergency landings. Hundreds of schools also received hoax bomb threats via email.

Dylan Browne, general manager of NATO's NCIA, said AI models would significantly help the alliance accelerate vulnerability discovery, detect emerging threats at machine speed and adopt countermeasures.

"For NATO, these technologies strengthen our cyber resilience, enhance our operational advantage and reinforce our ability to protect critical digital infrastructure at unprecedented scale and speed," he said.

The partnership marks OpenAI's latest foray into cybersecurity under the company's Daybreak program, through which enterprise customers and government agencies can gain access to its advanced models for authorized cybersecurity work.

The company said in September that Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation would use Daybreak to protect civilian infrastructure, providing access to tools to identify software vulnerabilities and develop and test fixes more quickly.
Meanwhile, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, ENISA, also used OpenAI models to identify vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions.
